A subsidy that cuts pollution per unit can still increase pollution overall. subsidies / has to be matched / by the contraction of the opportunity set of others. / The electricity companies' "freedom" is ③ decreased / at the expense of the ordinary individual, / who must suffer from increased taxation / to pay for the subsidy. Indeed, electricity prices may end up ⑤ lower / than they should be / and electricity consumption higher, / which will worsen global warming, / even though the emissions per unit of electricity / have been reduced. Power plants prefer subsidies for switching away from coal, but subsidies shift the costs to taxpayers and keep electricity prices too low, which can increase consumption and worsen global warming.

While classical economics assumes scarcity, the Star Trek world has little of it because technology provides everything, and generative AI may make our society similarly abundant.

But for someone to feel heard, / three things have to happen. / First, they have to feel like / the other person paid attention to what they said. / Second, they have to feel like / the other person understood what they said. / And third, the other person has to _________________.

Listening is not complete until the speaker can see that you listened. provided no response. / They might have attended to everything we said. / They might even have understood it completely. But without some sort of outward signal / that indicates they listened, / it's impossible to know / whether or not they actually did.
To make people feel heard, we must not only pay attention to them and understand them but also give an outward signal that shows we listened.

This intertwining of space, place, and experience / place and space are central to the very heart of experience, / we must accept the possibility / that the spatial framework is the medium of all experiences / — actions, thoughts, memories, and feelings of every place — / not merely a background or context exterior to experience / (as commonly supposed).

① with enough financial support for quality studies ② even in the absence of acceptance by other scientists ③ by tracing how science has developed throughout history ④ through a detailed examination of higher-level phenomena ⑤ without a complete accounting of what’s happening at all other levels No matter how you choose to delineate / your evolutionary system of interest / — let's say it's cell phones — / there will be some things / that your model just needs to take as a given, / such as the fact that new ideas emerge at particular times. Indeed, all models must make simplifying assumptions of this nature. / When Wallace and Darwin presented / their verbal model of biological evolution, / there was little knowledge / of how variation generation and inheritance worked. / They just took as a given / that these things happened somehow.

A good model does not have to explain everything to explain something well. simplifying assumptions. / Physicists, for example, must take as a given / the mass and charge of fundamental particles. / In a model of atomic bonds, / physicists don't attempt to explain / why electrons have their particular mass and charge, / they just accept the measured values and move on. The key point is that we can build useful models / at one level of analysis / ____________________________ (eee). without a complete accounting of what’s happening at all other
Every model takes some things as given, as Darwin did with inheritance and physicists do with particle mass, so useful models can be built at one level without fully explaining all other levels.

When people are collaborating face to face / they can easily see each other / and the range of different communication cues being used, / so the task space is a subset of the communication space. (B) Ishii, a professor at the MIT Media Lab, / describes this as seamless communication / because there is no functional separation / between the task and communication space. / However, when people are working remotely, / the task space is often separated / from the communication space.

Remote tools can connect us yet still split what we see from how we talk. have the face of their collaborator on one screen, / while looking at a shared document on another. / In this case, it is impossible to see / many of the remote collaborator's communication cues / at the same time as looking at the task space. when video conferencing਷ when they are video conferencing, while (A) So, there is an artificial seam / between the communication space and task space. / This is the type of impact / of remote communication technology / that needs to be predicted / through communication models.
In face-to-face work the task space lies within the communication space, but remote work separates them, creating an artificial seam that communication models need to predict.

Regardless of whether the statement was true or false, belief in the truth of the claim went up as a function of repetition. In 1977, psychologists Lynn Hasher and David Goldstein / asked a group of college students / how certain they were / that sixty general-knowledge trivia-like statements /were either true or false. / The students were asked to evaluate the sixty statements / three times, at two-week intervals. (① ) Crucially, only twenty of the statements were repeated each time; / the other forty were new. / ( ② ) The researchers then compared the 'truth-ratings' / of the repeated versus non-repeated statements. / ( ③ ) What they found was astonishing.

Repeating a claim does not make it true, but it makes it feel true. was true or false, / belief in the truth of the claim went up /as a function of repetition. (④ ) In other words, the more often you hear a statement, / the more 'true' it sounds. / ( ⑤ ) This became known / as the illusory truth effect.
In a 1977 study, students rated repeated statements as more true than new ones regardless of their actual truth, a result known as the illusory truth effect.

When submerged underwater, to avoid feeling the pressure of the surrounding environment, it is necessary to maintain the condition of equal external and internal pressure. The human body on the Earth's surface / experiences constant air pressure / equal to 16-18 tons per square meter of its body surface. / However, this pressure is not felt / because external pressure is balanced by internal pressure / in the lungs and air cavities of the body. (① ) During dives, in addition to atmospheric pressure, / the pressure of the water also acts on the human body. Divers stay safe by matching the pressure inside them to the pressure outside. avoid feeling the pressure of the surrounding environment, / it is necessary to maintain the condition / of equal external and internal pressure. ( ② ) To achieve this, / air or a breathing mixture is supplied to the diver / under pressure equal to the pressure / applied by the surrounding water. / ( ③ ) Water pressure increases proportionally with depth. It follows that a diver at a depth of 10 meters / experiences a pressure of 2 bar, / and to stabilize pressure, / the supply of a breathing mixture / under a pressure of 2 atmospheres / is required.
We do not feel air pressure because external and internal pressure are balanced, so divers must breathe air supplied at the same pressure as the surrounding water, which increases with depth.

Compared to those in peaceful areas, goldenrods in more hostile environments send more _______ understandable chemical messages, thereby _________ both the senders and the receivers. ① broadly … benefiting ② easily … harming ③ narrowly … protecting ④ accidentally … profiting ⑤ specifically … endangering Researchers recently found that goldenrods / that live in peaceful areas / without much threat from predators / will issue chemical alarm calls / that are incredibly specific / — comprehensible only to their close kin — / on the rare occasion they are attacked.

In dangerous times, sharing a warning widely helps the one who warns as much as those who are warned. neighbors / using chemical phrases / easily understood by all the goldenrod in the area, / not just their biological kin. / Instead of using coded whisper networks, / these goldenrod broadcast the threat over loudspeaker, / so to speak. broadly understandable It is the first time / research has confirmed that these chemical communications / are beneficial not only to the plant receiving them / but also to the sender. / When times are truly tough, / you do not want to be left standing in a field alone. / There will be no one to mate with, / no one to help bring in pollinators. benefiting both the senders and the receivers
Goldenrods in peaceful areas send alarm signals only their kin understand, but those in hostile areas send signals all neighbors can understand, which benefits both senders and receivers.
